title: Many Labs 5: Registered Multisite Replication of the Tempting-Fate Effects in Risen and Gilovich (2008)
overview: Replication of Risen & Gilovich (2008) Study 6: 2 (tempting fate) x 2 (cognitive load) between-subjects design; every original subject is replayed as one AI participant.

program.title: Many Labs 5: Registered Multisite Replication of the Tempting-Fate Effects in Risen and Gilovich (2008)

source.title: Many Labs 5: Registered Multisite Replication of the Tempting-Fate Effects in Risen and Gilovich (2008)
source.authors: Maya B. Mathur, Diane-Jo Bart-Plange, Balazs Aczel, et al., and Michael C. Frank
source.venue: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science

studies.title: Multisite replication of Risen & Gilovich (2008) Study 6 (tempting fate × cognitive load)
studies.description: Between-subjects 2 (tempting fate: tempted vs. not tempted) × 2 (cognitive load: counting backward vs. none) experiment run at 4 similar U.S. universities (updated protocol), 6 dissimilar universities, and on Amazon Mechanical Turk (RP:P protocol).

studies.title: Post hoc comparison with Many Labs 2 (analysis only)
studies.description: Reanalysis comparing this project's main-effect estimates with those of Many Labs 2 (Klein et al., 2018), using both projects' subject-level data; not an experiment.

evidence.quote: Risen and Gilovich (2008) found that subjects believed that “tempting fate” would be punished with ironic bad outcomes (a main effect), and that this effect was magnified when subjects were under cognitive load (an interaction).
We used four university sites (N = 754) chosen for similarity to the site of the original study to conduct a high-powered, preregistered replication focused primarily on the interaction effect.
That is, Risen and Gilovich hypothesized a positive interaction effect of cognitive load and tempting fate on the perceived likelihood of an ironic bad outcome.
Risen and Gilovich additionally hypothesized that deliberative thinking, also called System 2 processing
used a between-subjects factorial design to test these hypotheses

Subjects were randomly assigned to read a scenario in which they imagined themselves either having tempted fate by not having done the assigned reading or not having tempted fate by having done the assigned reading. Additionally, subjects’ cognitive load was manipulated by random assignment.

Subjects not under cognitive load simply read the scenario and then judged their likelihood of being called on in class (scale from 0 to 10). Subjects under cognitive load counted backward by 3s from a large number while reading the scenario and then provided the likelihood judgment.
The estimated difference in perceived likelihood of being called on in class
the difference in perceived likelihood was 1.54, 95% CI = [0.05, 3.03], p = .04
However, prior to the data collection for this previous replication effort, the authors of the original study expressed concerns about the protocol.
The previous replication (Frank & Mathur, 2016) found little evidence for either the main effect of tempting fate without cognitive load
Thus, this replication provided strong evidence for a main effect of tempting fate, albeit an effect of smaller magnitude than in the original study.
The protocol, sample-size criteria, exclusion criteria, and plan for statistical analysis were preregistered
All data, materials, and analysis code are publicly available at https://osf.io/h5a9y/.
Sites obtained ethics-committee approval when appropriate given their geographical location and institutional requirements, and data were collected in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

Our primary analyses used only data from university sites that were located in the United States and that met a criterion for being similar to the original site with respect to academic competitiveness (i.e., median SAT score > 90th percentile nationally); we refer to these sites as similar sites.
Subjects were undergraduates at Cornell University.
Subjects completed the experiment in controlled physical settings with reasonable isolation from other subjects (e.g., private lab room, private cubicles in a shared room).
RP:P replication protocol without modification to collect data from a new sample on MTurk.

Finally, we collected secondary data at several universities that did not meet the SAT criterion for similarity to Cornell or were located outside the United States; we refer to these sites as dissimilar sites.
At sites where subjects were not expected to speak fluent English, questionnaire materials were translated and then verified through independent back-translation.
The primary effects we statistically estimated were (a) the focal interaction effect within the similar sites and (b) the difference in this interaction between the similar sites and MTurk
Sample sizes were chosen to provide, in aggregate, more than 80% power to detect a three-way interaction with effect size (SMD) more than 0.75.
though in many cases this was not feasible.

Site-level and aggregate analyses were conducted by the first author, who was blinded to results until all the sites had completed data collection; these analyses were audited for accuracy by other authors.

we asked subjects assigned to cognitive load to use a scale from 0 to 10 to rate the perceived effort associated with the load task (“How much effort did the counting task require?”) and the task’s difficulty (“How difficult was the counting task?”).

These questions were also answered on a scale from 0 to 10.
we fit an ordinary least squares regression model of the perceived likelihood of being called on in class
This analysis approach is statistically equivalent to the analysis of variance model fit in the original study

fields.label: Method type
fields.value: Registered, preregistered multisite direct replication; between-subjects factorial experiment

fields.label: Summary
fields.value: Replicates Study 6 of Risen & Gilovich (2008): whether imagining having tempted fate raises the judged likelihood of an ironic bad outcome (being called on in class), and whether this is magnified by cognitive load. Run with an updated protocol at similar universities, at dissimilar universities, and on MTurk under the earlier RP:P protocol.

fields.label: Question
fields.value: Do people believe that tempting fate is punished with ironic bad outcomes, and is that belief stronger under cognitive load?

fields.label: Gap
fields.value: A previous MTurk replication (Frank & Mathur, 2016) failed to replicate both effects; the original authors had worried that cognitive load works less well online and that the scenario is less salient outside an elite university. Many Labs 2 replicated the main effect (smaller) but did not assess the interaction.

fields.label: Theory
fields.value: Deliberative (System 2) thinking may suppress irrational tempting-fate heuristics, so cognitive load should magnify the effect.

nodes.title: H1: main effect of tempting fate

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Subjects who imagine having tempted fate judge an ironic bad outcome (being called on in class) as more likely than subjects who have not tempted fate. Tested in subjects not under cognitive load; reported as the main effect.

nodes.title: H2 (focal): Tempting Fate × Cognitive Load interaction

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Positive interaction of cognitive load and tempting fate on the perceived likelihood of an ironic bad outcome.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: The primary replication test is the interaction within the similar sites, and its difference from MTurk (three-way interaction).

fields.value: Read scenario, counting task (load conditions), likelihood judgment, and the four 0–10 secondary measures can be replayed as text. Blocked until the scenario, counting-task instruction and exact item wording are supplied (not printed in the paper).

fields.value: One AI participant per original subject; no scripted roles.

fields.label: Conditions
fields.value: Four cells (tempting fate × cognitive load). Site type, language and lab setting cannot be varied faithfully for text-only AI participants; the primary replay target is the similar-site, English population.

fields.label: Outcomes
fields.value: Likelihood rating 0–10; secondary ratings. Cognitive load is only nominal for a text model: counting backward cannot occupy working memory, so any load effect is not comparable with human subjects.

fields.label: Limits
fields.value: Physical lab context, real distraction and compensation cannot be reproduced. Agreement with the paper would not show that people behave the same way.

nodes.title: Comparison of main effect with Many Labs 2

fields.label: Aim
fields.value: Explore why Many Labs 2 found a main effect while this project did not.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: Compared U.S. MTurk samples; reanalysed raw Many Labs 2 data with LMM, GEE and raw mean differences; redefined sampling frames; pooled main effect across primary-analysis sites.

fields.label: Inputs
fields.value: Subject-level data of Many Labs 5 and Many Labs 2 (primary-analysis sites; load-condition subjects of this project excluded).

fields.label: Protocol differences
fields.value: Likelihood scale 0–10 (11 options) in Many Labs 5 vs 1–10 in Many Labs 2; skipping allowed in Many Labs 2; Many Labs 2 ran it within a 30-minute randomized block.

fields.label: result_kind
fields.value: reported

fields.label: Difference
fields.value: Many Labs 5 main effect smaller than Many Labs 2: LMM −0.44 [−0.92, 0.04], p = .07; discrepancy remained unexplained; pooled estimate showed a small main effect.

fields.label: Many Labs 2 as cited
fields.value: Main effect strongly supported in Many Labs 2 but smaller than in the original.

steps.title: Random assignment to scenario and load condition
Read the imagined class scenario (tempted or not tempted fate)
Read scenario: not having done the assigned reading (tempted fate)
Read scenario: having done the assigned reading (not tempted fate)
Count backward by 3s from a large number while reading

rule.label: Concurrency with reading
rule.value: Counting occurs while reading the scenario; further timing rules not stated.

steps.title: Judge the likelihood of being called on in class (0–10)
Rate effort and difficulty of the counting task (load conditions only)
Rate importance of answering correctly and negativity of answering incorrectly
Report the ending number and the reading/counting effort split (load conditions only)

issues.title: Number recruited not reported
issues.reason: Only analysed and excluded counts are in Table 2.
issues.suggestedAction: Take from the OSF data or leave as is.

issues.title: A priori exclusion criteria not listed in the paper
issues.reason: The paper refers to preregistered criteria without stating them.
issues.impact: Exclusion rules cannot be applied to AI participants.

issues.title: Per-condition sample sizes not reported
issues.reason: Only per-site analysed n is given.

issues.title: Randomization procedure and allocation ratio not stated
issues.reason: The paper says random assignment only.
issues.impact: Assignment in replay must use an implementation choice (equal allocation).
issues.suggestedAction: Confirm equal allocation or supply the procedure.

issues.title: Consent text not supplied
issues.reason: The questionnaire PDF shows the consent screen only as the placeholder “(Insert consent text here.)”.
issues.impact: Consent wording is unknown; it is not part of the replay prompt.
issues.suggestedAction: Supply the site consent text if it should be shown to participants.

issues.title: Timing rule of counting task relative to reading
issues.reason: The paper says 'while reading' but gives no further rule (e.g., duration, response mode).
issues.impact: Concurrency cannot be reproduced exactly in text.

issues.title: Many Labs 2 raw data not supplied
issues.reason: The s2 reanalysis uses raw Many Labs 2 data that is not in the paper.
issues.impact: The s2 analysis cannot be re-run.
issues.suggestedAction: Supply the data in sources/ if needed.

issues.title: Importance item wording differs between the paper and the questionnaire
issues.reason: The paper quotes “in the scenario you just read about, how important would it be for you…”; the questionnaire prints “in the class you just read about, how important would it be to you…”.
issues.impact: The replay uses the printed questionnaire wording.
issues.suggestedAction: Confirm that the printed questionnaire is the version that was administered.

issues.title: Protocol says new items come last; questionnaire prints difficulty and effort earlier
issues.reason: The protocol says the new items appear at the very end; in the printed questionnaire the difficulty and effort items follow the end-number question on page 3 and only importance and negativity are last.
issues.impact: The replay follows the printed page order.

readiness.note: Scenario texts, counting-task directions, start number and likelihood item are transcribed verbatim from sources/RG_questionnaire_items.pdf; remaining open issues are checks.
